title: Kegs and the cooler
lead: Keg sizes and what they pour, the walk-in, CO2 safety and receiving beer.

sections.name: Receiving and freshness

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Check it in, rotate it, keep it cold.

sections.source: Brewers Association / CraftBeer.com, Beer & Food Course; Cicerone, Advanced Cicerone Syllabus v6.0 and exam page (cicerone.org)

read.bigIdea: Every keg has a number of pours.
read.where: From the Brewers Association: a **half barrel** is **15.5 gallons** (1,984 oz, about **124 pints** or 165 12-oz pours); a **quarter** is **7.75 gallons** (about **62 pints**); a **sixtel** is **5.16 gallons** (about **41 pints**); a **50-liter Euro** keg is 13.2 gallons (about 105 pints). A “slim quarter” holds the same as a quarter but is tall and narrow. **Imported** kegs often don’t take the standard US coupler, so check when ordering.
read.mixup: “Pony keg” is used loosely: some mean a quarter, some an eighth. Ask for gallons.

read.bigIdea: The cooler is the draft system’s heart.
read.where: Check the walk-in every day: thermometers at **36–38°F**, lines full with no bubbles or kinks, no leaks, gas valves open, and listen for a hiss. A keg that sat out warms fast (38°F to 48°F in about 6 hours) and takes most of a **day** to chill back. Kegs on tap longer than **45 days** may no longer taste as the brewer meant. Keep **food** away from kegs and lines; a dedicated beer cooler is best.
read.mixup: A keg can feel cold on the outside and still be warm inside. Give it time.

keyPoints.line: a full half barrel: lift in pairs.
CO2 pools low and can kill.

read.bigIdea: Kegs are heavy; CO2 is dangerous.
read.where: A full half barrel weighs about **161 lb**: lift with a partner or a lift, and never get below a rolling keg. Kegs are pressure vessels: **never** take a keg valve apart. **CO2 tanks** never go **inside the walk-in**: CO2 is colorless, odorless and **heavier than air**, so a leak fills the room from the floor up, and at high levels it can kill in minutes. Store tanks **upright and chained**, valve cap on. The Brewers Association recommends a **CO2 alarm** in walk-ins with gas lines.
read.mixup: A tank’s gauge doesn’t show how full it is: pressure changes with temperature. Weigh it.

read.bigIdea: Freshness starts at the back door.
read.where: When beer arrives, check the **invoice** against what came, that **date codes** are readable and in range, and that crowns, cans and keg valves are clean; **refuse** anything wrong and get the rest **straight into the cold**. The **3-30-300** rule (MillerCoors research, quoted by the Brewers Association): **3 days** at 90°F, **30 days** at room temperature and **300 days** cold do about the same damage. Rotate **first in, first out**.
read.mixup: A case left on a warm dock for an afternoon has lost real shelf life, even back in the cooler.
